newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH MPS MAY SEEK RIDER ON GERMAN POST-WW2 PACT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH MPS MAY SEEK RIDER ON GERMAN POST-WW2 PACT.

text.p: The largest Czech opposition party, the Social Democrats (CSSD), said on Monday that it may want an appendix added to a Czech-German post-World War Two declaration expected to be signed soon.

The Czech Republic and Germany in December concluded nearly two years of sensitive negotiations over the text of the joint declaration aiming for political closure to questions lingering from World War Two and its aftermath.
The declaration expresses Bonn's sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague's regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of ethnic Germans.
The text has been approved by both governments, which have each said it should not be reopened by their parliaments.
It is expected to be signed by both countries' prime ministers and presidents in the coming weeks.

But Petr Sulak, a CSSD deputy and member of the foreign committee of the Czech parliament's lower house which must ratify the agreement, told Reuters on Monday that his party still had concerns about the text.
"The Social Democrats have remarks to certain formulations in the declaration which could in the future be a basis for negative tendencies from the German side," he said.
The CSSD has expressed conditional support for the text, but has been relunctant to announce its full support.
Sulak declined to elaborate on what particular passages the party found troublesome, but he did say the problem did not include property issues.

"(CSSD) will discuss the text, adopt conslusions and will want it to be shown in the debate over text in the parliament and later possibly seen in an additional statement to the declaration approved by the parliament," he said.
The other two opposition parties in Czech parliament, the ultra-right Republicans and the little-reformed Communists, have both categorically rejected the pact with Germany.
The government of Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus is two seats short of a majority in the lower house.
Diplomats have said that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is expected to visit Prague later this month to sign the document with Klaus, but a firm date has not been confirmed.
The parliaments of the two countries are then expected to discuss the text in February ahead of a formal ceremony of ratification including both countries' presidents.
The chairman of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD). Oskar Lafontaine, said on a recent visit to Prague that his party would push for approval of the decalration.

Czech opponents of the text claim it fails to pay direct compensation to victims of Nazi agression, while German groups are furious that it avoids paying restitution for Prague's expropriation of property of the so-called Sudeten Germans.
